latent.whyUnnamed: A digest carries no label. The person holding one believes it is the checksum, singular, so the possibility that they are comparing two different algorithms never becomes a thought, let alone a query.

latent.whyUnnamed: A UUID looks correct to a human at every level except the two bits that encode its version and variant. Nobody searches for a checker because nobody can see the thing that is wrong, and the rejection downstream almost never says wrong UUID version.

opportunities.title: Cron to systemd Timer Converter
opportunities.problem: I am moving cron jobs onto systemd timers and have to hand-translate each crontab line into an OnCalendar expression, with no way to check that the translation fires at the same moments.
opportunities.workflow: a date/time → Schedule Expression Translation → a date/time
searchQueries: convert crontab line to systemd timer OnCalendar
systemd timer equivalent of cron expression
existingSolutions: systemd-analyze calendar on a machine you already have
blog posts with a handful of worked examples
solutionWeaknesses: systemd-analyze only checks an OnCalendar you have already written, it does not translate a crontab line
man pages document the grammar and never compare it to cron
worked examples cover the easy schedules and stop exactly where the semantics diverge
userFailures: translates '0 0 * * 0' to 'OnCalendar=weekly' and does not notice weekly means Monday in systemd and Sunday in cron
writes '*/7' expecting every seventh day and gets a step that restarts at each month boundary in cron but not in systemd
translates a crontab line that used both day-of-month and day-of-week without knowing cron ORs those two fields while systemd ANDs them
forgets the timer inherits the system timezone rather than the crontab's TZ variable, so everything shifts by hours after a DST change

latent.whyUnnamed: Nobody searches for a translation checker, because the moment you would want one is the moment you still believe your translation is right. The search that does happen is for the syntax, and the syntax is not the part that goes wrong.
observedBehaviour: People hand-translate crontab lines into OnCalendar and confirm the unit loads, which proves the syntax parses and says nothing about when it fires.
They run systemd-analyze calendar on the result and read the next elapse, then compare it against the old cron schedule from memory.
The mistranslation is discovered weeks later, when a backup that was supposed to run on Sunday has been running on Monday.

opportunities.title: Shell Quote Escalator
opportunities.problem: I need to send a command through several layers that each strip one level of quoting (a local shell, then ssh, then sudo or docker exec), and I cannot tell what the far end will actually receive until it runs.

existingSolutions: trial and error against the real server
answers on Q and A sites for one specific command shape
solutionWeaknesses: trial and error runs the wrong command on a real machine to find out it was wrong
shlex.quote handles one layer and the problem is that there are several
every answer is pinned to one command and does not generalize to the next one
userFailures: adds backslashes until the command stops erroring, without ever seeing what the far end received
writes a glob or a $VAR expecting the remote side to expand it and gets it expanded locally instead, silently, against the wrong filesystem
gets a path with a space split into two arguments three layers down and deletes something adjacent to the intended target
escapes correctly for bash and ships it to a host whose login shell is not bash

latent.whyUnnamed: The thing has no name. People do not experience it as 'multi-layer shell quoting', they experience it as the command not working, so what they type into a search box is their one command rather than the class of problem it belongs to.
observedBehaviour: People add a backslash, re-run against the real server, and repeat until the error stops, using production as the test harness.
They paste the command into a chat channel and ask a colleague to count the quoting levels by eye.
They give up on quoting entirely and base64 the whole command, which works and leaves nobody able to read what the automation runs.
